Title: 'Ableitung der Fundamentalgleichung' (derivation of the fundamental equation). The fundamental equation is the addition theorem for the general elliptic function x = f(z) obtained by inverting a quartic integral with only even powers.

Setup. Let x = f(z) and y = f(z+m) = f(w), where z = ∫ dx/√(A+Bx²+Cx⁴). Since dw = dz, both satisfy
 dz = dx/√(A+Bx²+Cx⁴) = dy/√(A+By²+Cy⁴).
The common independent variable is called t, so z = t + const and w = t + m + const. Primes denote d/dt.

(1) First-order equations: x'² = A+Bx²+Cx⁴ and y'² = A+By²+Cy⁴.

(2) Second-order equations. Differentiating gives 2x'x'' = (2Bx+4Cx³)x'. Dividing by 2x' (my step) gives x'' = Bx+2Cx³; likewise y'' = By+2Cy³.

(3) Combination of the first-order equations: x²y'² − y²x'² = A(x²−y²) − Cx²y²(x²−y²) = (A − Cx²y²)(x²−y²).

(4) Combination of the second-order equations: y x'' − x y'' = 2Cxy(x²−y²).

(5) Dividing (4) by yx'−xy'. Implicit step (mine): x²y'²−y²x'² = (xy'−yx')(xy'+yx'). Hence yx'−xy' = −(A−Cx²y²)(x²−y²)/(yx'+xy'). Therefore
 (yx''−xy'')/(yx'−xy') = −2Cxy(yx'+xy')/(A−Cx²y²).

(6) Recognising both sides as logarithmic derivatives (implicit, mine):
- The left side is d/dt log(yx'−xy'), since d/dt(yx'−xy') = yx''−xy''.
- The right side is d/dt log(A−Cx²y²), since d/dt(A−Cx²y²) = −2Cxy(xy'+yx').
Integrating gives log(yx'−xy') = log(A−Cx²y²) + Const. Equivalently, (yx'−xy')/(A−Cx²y²) is constant along the motion.

(7) Evaluating the constant. Take the point where x = 0, i.e. z = 0, with f(0) = 0 implicitly. There y = M = f(m), x' = √A (sign convention), and y' = √(A+BM²+CM⁴). The constant is (M√A − 0)/A = M/√A = f(m)/√A.

(8) Result. Write fz' for y, so m = z'−z. Then
 f(z'−z) = √A·[ f(z')√(A+Bf(z)²+Cf(z)⁴) − f(z)√(A+Bf(z')²+Cf(z')⁴) ] / (A − C f(z)² f(z')²).
This is the subtraction (equivalently addition) theorem for the elliptic function. With A = 1, B = −(1+k²), C = k² it is the Jacobi formula
 sn(u−v) = (sn u cn v dn v − sn v cn u dn u)/(1 − k² sn²u sn²v).
The page serves the surrounding work (theta series p, q, r on the previous page; transformation of elliptic integrals on the next page) by providing the basic algebraic addition law.
errors: No mathematical errors. Every step checks: x''=Bx+2Cx³; x²y'²−y²x'²=(A−Cx²y²)(x²−y²); yx''−xy''=2Cxy(x²−y²); the quotient formula; and the integration to (yx'−xy')/(A−Cx²y²)=const.
Minor implicit assumptions: f(0)=0, the sign choice x'(0)=+√A, and the branch of the square roots. The variable t is used without being defined; it stands for z (equivalently w−m).
Notational slip only: y' is written ∂y/dt.

results.what: Addition/subtraction theorem for the inverse function of ∫dx/√(A+Bx²+Cx⁴): f(z'−z) = √A[f z'·√(A+Bfz²+Cfz⁴) − fz·√(A+Bfz'²+Cfz'⁴)]/(A − C fz² fz'²)
results.modern_name: Addition theorem for elliptic functions (Jacobi sn addition formula; Euler's addition theorem for elliptic integrals)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (1750s, addition theorem for elliptic integrals); in sn form Abel/Jacobi (1827–29)

results.what: Derivation via the invariant (yx'−xy')/(A−Cx²y²): differentiate the first-order ODEs and identify both sides of the quotient as logarithmic derivatives
results.modern_name: Euler's differential-equation proof of the addition theorem (as reproduced e.g. in Whittaker–Watson §22.2)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's possession of the addition theorems for lemniscatic and general elliptic functions (from about 1797–1800) is well documented. The proof method is the classical Euler-type invariant argument. This is a clean but routine derivation.

checkable.asserts: d/dt(A−Cx²y²) = −2Cxy(yx'+xy'), so the right side is a logarithmic derivative

checkable.sympy: from mpmath import ellipfun, sqrt; k=0.6; m=k**2; u,v=0.7,0.3; s=lambda a: ellipfun('sn',a,m=m); c=lambda a: ellipfun('cn',a,m=m); d=lambda a: ellipfun('dn',a,m=m); abs(s(u-v)-(s(u)*c(v)*d(v)-s(v)*c(u)*d(u))/(1-m*s(u)**2*s(v)**2))<1e-12
checkable.asserts: Gauss's final formula with A=1, B=−(1+k²), C=k² (f=sn, z'=u, z=v) is the sn subtraction formula
